prompt:
Which listed dependency is a **trivial FD**? Each option is written in this form:

```formula
X → Y
where
X, Y: sets of attributes; {sid, cid} means the two attributes together
→: functionally determines: rows that agree on X agree on Y
In words: X's values fix Y's values. The attributes are sid (student id), cid (course code), sname (student name), ctitle (course title) and grade.
```

options.text:
```formula
{sid, cid} → cid
where
sid: student identifier
cid: course code
→: functional determination; equal left values require equal right values
{ }: a set, with no duplicates or ordering
In words: The student/course pair fixes its course code.
```
options.explanation: Correct. The right side is a subset of the left side, so it holds in every relation by reflexivity and tells you nothing.

options.text:
```formula
{sid, cid} → grade
where
sid: student identifier
cid: course code
grade: the student’s grade on that course
→: functional determination; equal left values require equal right values
{ }: a set, with no duplicates or ordering
In words: The student/course pair fixes the grade.
```
options.explanation: Non-trivial: grade is not among the left-hand attributes.

options.text:
```formula
sid → sname
where
sid: student identifier
sname: student name
→: functional determination; equal left values require equal right values
In words: The student id fixes the student name.
```
options.explanation: Non-trivial: sname is not part of {sid}, so this states a real business rule.

options.text:
```formula
cid → {cid, ctitle}
where
cid: course code
ctitle: course title
→: functional determination; equal left values require equal right values
{ }: a set, with no duplicates or ordering
In words: The course code fixes itself and the course title.
```
options.explanation: Not trivial, because ctitle is not on the left. (Its cid part is trivial, but the FD as a whole is not.)

workedExample:
An FD is trivial exactly when its right side is a subset of its left side:

```formula
{sname} ⊄ {sid}
{grade} ⊄ {sid, cid}
{cid} ⊆ {sid, cid}
{cid, ctitle} ⊄ {cid}
where
⊆: is a subset of: every attribute on the left also appears on the right
⊄: is not a subset of
{ }: a set of attributes
sid, cid, sname, ctitle, grade: student id, course code, student name, course title, grade
In words: X → Y is trivial exactly when Y ⊆ X. Only {sid, cid} → cid has its right side inside its left side, so it is the trivial one.
```

Trivial FDs come free from Armstrong's reflexivity rule.

prompt:
A table currently holds these synthetic test rows, including a deliberately inconsistent M1/Leeds entry. Treat the listed values as data to audit, rather than a claim about postal geography:

```
zip    city      street
SW1A   London    Mall
SW1A   London    Horse Gds
M1     Manchstr  Oxford Rd
M1     Leeds     Albion St
```

Which statement about the intended dependency as a constraint on all legal states is justified by this data alone? The options use functional-dependency notation:

```formula
X → Y
where
X, Y: attributes of the table
→: functionally determines: any two rows that agree on X must agree on Y
In words: "zip → city" claims that a postcode district fixes the city.
```

options.text: The postcode district fixes the city as a valid business rule
options.explanation: The two M1 rows agree on zip but disagree on city, so this FD is violated here (or the data is dirty).

options.text: The business rule that city determines zip is proved by these rows
options.explanation: The data contains no counterexample, but a lack of counterexamples never proves an FD. It is a rule only if the business says so.

options.text: The business rule that street determines zip is proved because every street here is different
options.explanation: Unique values in a sample do not make an FD a rule; two towns can each have an Oxford Road.

options.text: The data refutes the postcode-to-city dependency: equal districts have different cities
options.explanation: Correct. The two M1 rows have the same postcode-district value but different city values, refuting that dependency on this stored state.

workedExample:
1. To refute a functional dependency, find two relational tuples equal on its determinant but different on its right side.
2. The two M1 rows:

```formula
t_1[zip] = t_2[zip] = 'M1'
t_1[city] = 'Manchstr'
t_2[city] = 'Leeds'
where
t_1, t_2: the third and fourth rows of the table
t_1[zip], t_2[zip]: each row's zip value; t_1[city], t_2[city] likewise for city
zip, city: the postcode-district and city attributes
'M1', 'Manchstr', 'Leeds': the literal values in the data
In words: two rows agree on zip but disagree on city, so zip → city is violated (→ means "functionally determines").
```

3. For the proposed city-to-district and street-to-district rules there is no counterexample, but that is all you can say. Data can disprove an FD, never prove one.
4. In practice: either the FD is a genuine rule and a row is wrong (fix it), or the FD was never true (do not design around it).

prompt:
A colleague argues: “If a student and course together fix the grade, the student alone must fix it too.” Which tiny instance shows this inference is invalid? Tuples are written (sid, cid, grade).

```formula
{sid, cid} → grade
sid → grade
where
sid: the student id
cid: the course code
grade: the grade on that course
→: functionally determines: rows that agree on the left side agree on the right side
{ }: a set of attributes: sid and cid together
In words: line 1 says the pair (student, course) fixes the grade; line 2 claims the student alone fixes it.
```

options.explanation: Correct. The student/course pairs differ, so the premise is satisfied; the student is the same and grades differ, so the student-alone conclusion fails.
These are the same relational tuple (a relation is a set), and they agree on everything, so nothing is violated.
These have different students, so they do not refute the student-alone conclusion.
The student/course pair is the same but grades differ, so this violates the premise itself.

workedExample:
To refute an inference, construct a relation satisfying its premise but violating its conclusion.

1. Premise: each student/course pair has one grade.
2. Target: same student, different grades on different courses.
3. Use two different courses so the premise is not violated:

```
sid cid grade
 1  DB   A
 1  OS   B
```

4. The premise holds, the target fails, so the inference is invalid. The left side of an FD cannot be split.
